reasoning_details.text:
I need to find a single structural change targeting M and L. The key is what sits in L2 by the end of execution — outputs written with evict_last persist there and get written back after the timing window closes, so maximizing dirty output in L2 (rather than input data) at the end should help, since with 126 MB L2 the last chunk of output tends to stay resident. I'm weighing whether loading inputs with evict_first instead would push input data out faster, though that seems to cost L a measurable hit on A100.

Tried evict_first on loads with nc hint — marginal gain on B200 but not worth repeating. There's a bigger issue: the harness flush leaves L2 full of dirty zero-buffer lines, and our kernel's reads will evict those, triggering writebacks inside our timed window. Since L2 is the point of coherence for DRAM traffic, there's likely no way to read without allocating in L2 and forcing that eviction, so this writeback cost seems unavoidable for larger workloads.

I wonder whether write-back compression or zero-fill detection on the B200's L2 is masking the expected savings. I'm also considering whether reordering processing so outputs stay protected in L2 via evict_last while inputs default could minimize DRAM write traffic within the window, though reads still need accounting for in the 805 MB L figure.

I'm now questioning whether evict_last persisting lines are capped by some hardware-governed fraction of L2, similar to cudaLimitPersistingL2CacheSize on Ampere, which would explain why full L2 coverage from evict_last stores isn't being achieved.

Then I shift to checking whether tile iteration order (Q-major vs K-major) matters structurally, before focusing on the 100-200 MB range: with 100 MB total and 50 MB output, I'd expect reads alone to hit near 6.7 µs plus overhead for roughly 10 µs if writes were fully hidden, but the measured 16.4 µs suggests writes aren't being hidden as well as hoped.

I'm realizing the actual culprit may be the persisting-flush interaction: when our kernel allocates 100 MB of lines in an L2 full of dirty flush data, that whole 100 MB gets written back as flush eviction traffic, so total window traffic becomes 50 MB reads plus 100 MB flush writebacks (150 MB), rather than the cleaner 50+50 split I was assuming.

With evict_last, the measured write traffic matches ~100 MB of flush writeback; if inputs were evict_first instead and replaced each other preferentially, flush eviction should drop to just 50 MB for outputs, saving significant cycles -- but the r6-s-ldef-nc-disp measurements (19.0 vs 19.1) show no such improvement, meaning evict_first loads aren't actually preferring to replace each other, or the zero_ memset kernel isn't using evict_first-style stores at all. I also consider whether B200's L2 has some zero-line compression trick, but that seems unlikely for standard allocations, so I'm still hunting for what the real remaining lever is.

Since I notice the test harness actually runs on a rented B200 GPU rather than a simulator, I realize I can directly measure real hardware effects with my limited GPU call budget, so I start sketching a few concrete experiments: using evict_first cache hints on loads paired with evict_last stores (similar to what was already tried), exploring a fractional L2::evict_unchanged policy, and considering discarding input cache lines via L2 discard instructions right after reading them since we technically own those input tensors during the kernel.

But thinking about discard.global.L2 more carefully, I recognize it actually makes the memory contents undefined rather than just freeing cache space cleanly — it behaves like a weak write of an indeterminate value, which means it would corrupt the input tensor data. That's risky since the harness might reuse or validate against those inputs, making this approach too close to a correctness violation to rely on.

Other options I'm weighing: priority demotion via applypriority (not useful), no-allocate stores (irrelevant), prefetching later tiles into L2 with cp.async.bulk.prefetch, or reordering how CTAs process Q versus K tiles so both streams interleave for better DRAM locality — right now most active CTAs are locked into one stream at a time.

I'm also considering the kernel's tail behavior: the timing window closes when stores are acknowledged by L2, not DRAM, so whatever hasn't been written back by then stays retained. If L2 has limited capacity for dirty lines, I need to estimate what fraction of the 100 MB output could be retained versus flushed, comparing against the measured 16.4 µs and 17.9 µs baseline timings to back out that retention fraction.

Given the uncertainty about whether writebacks for the zeroed flush buffer actually occur within my measurement window, I think the cleanest path forward is empirical testing on a rented B200 rather than continuing to reason from first principles about L2 eviction policy and compression behavior.

Other pairing variants like r6-ldg256-qkpair and r4-cuda-ldg256-token performed similarly to what's already been tried. I'm now considering DRAM read/write turnaround costs—mixing reads and writes hurts efficiency, and the timing of L2 writebacks relative to the eviction window matters. Thinking through what actually occupies L2 by the end of the kernel: mostly our outputs still pending eviction.

I'm estimating the math here: inputs stay in L2 as normal cache lines while outputs use evict_last, competing for the same space. If inputs were evict_first instead, they'd take up less room, leaving more L2 capacity for retained output, which should shrink the writeback window. Testing r6 with nc+evict_first only yielded a marginal ~0.4-0.5% gain for the L case, and working through the numbers—805 MB at theoretical vs achieved bandwidth—suggests only about 50 MB of output is actually being retained in L2, far short of the ~126 MB I'd expect if nearly all of L2 were available. So something else is eating that capacity, whether it's input lines, flush lines, or some cap on evict_last retention, and I want to figure out what's consuming the rest.

I'm considering a few explanations: maybe B200's dual-die L2 only effectively gives 126 MB per partition and data gets duplicated or homed oddly across dies, similar to how H100 handles near/far caching; maybe hardware caps how much of each set evict_last lines can occupy to prevent starvation; or maybe input tensors are simply taking up more room than I assumed. I should test this directly on a rented B200 by comparing eviction policies on the loads, though I need to check which variants have already been tried (like r6-s-ldef-nc-disp with its roughly 5.4/19.0/75.4 timings) so I don't duplicate work.

Since those numbers nearly match the parent's baseline, evict_first for inputs doesn't seem to be making a measurable difference, which rules out input eviction as the bottleneck. I'm also wondering if the L2 is proactively writing back dirty evict_last lines whenever the DRAM bus goes idle, which would shrink effective retention, or if there's some quirk with how flush lines were memset that avoids triggering evictions. Given limited time, I think the most productive next step is to try store-side eviction policy variants directly on the rented B200, since PTX supports eviction priority qualifiers on stores similar to loads.

So any gains above physical throughput thanks to retention must come from improved physical efficiency, since mixed read+write DRAM access tends to run lower efficiency than read-only streams. That makes me wonder if writes during the retention window are the bottleneck, while writes afterward aren't, since retention itself is capped by L2 capacity.

I'm also wondering whether flush-line dirty writebacks falling inside the window would add a huge unavoidable cost, unless evictions get absorbed by our own lines victimizing each other -- though the measured gain from that approach was tiny, suggesting the flush lines might not actually be dirty during the window for some reason tied to L2 write-back timing. Rather than keep theorizing, I think the fastest path is to just empirically test a few variants on the rented B200 and pick whichever performs best.

I'm sketching out several candidate changes to try: adjusting the cache eviction policy on stores/loads, reversing processing order, tweaking the fractional eviction policy for stores, marking loads with no-allocate to avoid L1 pollution, and restructuring the MLP kernel so each thread handles more rows to keep more data in flight per SM. I want to figure out which of these structural changes is most likely to matter before running tests.

I'm also considering the dual-die L2 topology issue — some SMs writing to addresses homed on the other die's L2 slice, which isn't really controllable — and wondering whether reordering work so stores dominate the kernel's tail changes anything, though it probably doesn't. Another angle: at kernel start, L2 is likely full of dirty flushed lines from the prior run, so the first chunk of our allocations may trigger writeback traffic as those lines get evicted, which could affect timing in a way distinct from the steady-state behavior later in the kernel.

Checking the other scale points: at 805 MB the gap between r3 and r5 narrows to only about 2 µs, which is smaller than expected. At 100 MB it's similarly modest, around 1.5 µs — suggesting the benefit shrinks at these sizes rather than scaling consistently.

Working through the DRAM traffic math at M with no-hint versus evict_last: if the full 100 MB flush writeback were actually happening, total traffic would be 150 MB, implying an impossible 11.2 TB/s bandwidth. Since the observed 13.4 µs only supports about 100.7 MB of traffic (7.5 TB/s), that means the flush writebacks aren't fully occurring as I assumed — something else must be going on with how those lines are being handled.

Maybe L2 proactively cleans dirty lines in the background rather than waiting for eviction pressure, which would explain the extra write traffic even though kernel completion itself doesn't trigger a flush.

I can't settle this through reasoning alone, so I should test it experimentally, though my budget is limited. Worth considering: a persistent grid with strided tile processing per CTA, or having each thread handle two rows for more bytes in flight.

The ldg256-token-r2 variant without stel showed essentially no gain over r3 (5.9/22.4/79.2 vs 6.0/22.6/79.3), confirming the MLP is saturated. That leaves cache policy variants as the only lever that's shown real impact — worth trying different evict_last/evict_first combinations for stores, cache hint policies, no_allocate flags, and corresponding load-side variants like evict_first or evict_unchanged hints.

I'm also wondering about applypriority or discard instructions on L2, though discard would wreck output lines. The real question is write-allocate behavior — a full 256-bit store filling a 32-byte sector shouldn't need a DRAM read-back, so that's fine. But the bigger suspicion is that L2 starts with ~126 MB of dirty flush lines, and our ~100 MB footprint is evicting most of them, forcing writebacks — except the math doesn't add up (150 MB in 13.4 µs implies an impossible 11 TB/s), so either the flush lines are mostly clean or something else is going on.

I'm computing marginal bandwidth across size bands: from 12.6 MB up through 805 MB, the marginal rate settles around 7.0 TB/s above 200 MB, but sits higher (7.5-7.9 TB/s) at smaller sizes — suggesting some writes are being retained rather than flushed at smaller footprints.

Checking whether fitting a fixed overhead plus a 7.0 TB/s rate against the data points explains the extra time seen at smaller sizes, the residual fixed cost grows as size shrinks, hinting at a constant per-call overhead layered on top of bandwidth.

I'm realizing the apparent retention effect is actually tiny, only around 15 MB rather than the full 126 MB L2 size, meaning there's a much bigger opportunity to retain far more of the output and shave off latency at larger sizes if that retention could be scaled up.

Now I'm questioning why retention caps at roughly 15 MB — maybe evict_last has a limited effective capacity, or dirty lines get written back eagerly, or input/flush lines are eating the space. I'm cross-checking the numbers at the M size and the no-hint case to see if input lines alone could explain the discrepancy.

I think the best path forward is to run actual experiments on the rented B200 to test cache policies that might boost retention — starting with trying an evict_first hint variant and seeing how it affects all 16 workloads.

I'm wondering whether evict_last is "sticky" in a way that caps occupancy, which would keep retention similar to normal LRU. With evict_first on early tiles the behavior matches what already happens on writeback anyway, so limiting evict_last to just the last chunk of output wouldn't change much.

Then I'm recalling that on Ampere, evict_last lines are actually governed by the persisting L2 set-aside size (cudaLimitPersistingL2CacheSize) through the access policy window — if that set-aside defaults to zero, evict_last hints might just degrade to normal priority, which would explain why retention caps around the observed size instead of scaling with evict_last usage.

Since I can't manipulate environment limits, I'm pivoting toward making inputs evict_first so they get evicted preferentially over normal-priority outputs, trying to recall how r6's non-coherent load path with no-allocate and evict_first performed on the rented B200.

The r6 numbers came out nearly identical to r5, suggesting neither priority policy retains much data, likely because B200's L2 eagerly drains dirty lines during idle DRAM write slots regardless of hints. If retention beyond the output tail is essentially impossible, the real remaining lever is physical efficiency around the 86% plateau — maybe grouping read-heavy and write-heavy phases to reduce DRAM turnaround costs.

Since I have the rented B200 available, it's worth running actual experiments rather than theorizing further. I'm considering a few candidates: tweaking cache-hint combinations on stores/loads/weights, or restructuring to use 2 tiles per CTA to cut CTA launch overhead per byte, which would roughly halve the CTA count for the L matrix.

Thinking about the CTA launch overhead more carefully — with short-lived CTAs (~1-2µs) and relaunch gaps in the hundreds of nanoseconds, there's maybe a 10% loss in bytes-in-flight during the turnaround. More concurrent CTAs could compensate, but the earlier 2-rows-per-thread variant didn't beat the 3-row version, suggesting we're already near saturation. I'm now wondering if there's a way to hide the store-to-exit latency instead.

I'm reconsidering whether L2 compression could explain the discrepancy, but since Torch allocations don't use the compression flag that cuMemCreate offers on B200, that's probably not it. Looking at the r5 results against the theoretical 7 TB/s ceiling, the small-workload case floors out around 1.8-2.5x the ideal, consistent with a fixed kernel-launch overhead rather than bandwidth limits. The task hints at focusing on M and L sizes and what's sitting in L2 right as the kernel finishes, so I should think through what residual state remains in cache at that point.

At kernel end, L2 holds the tail of input lines still resident from normal reads, plus output lines written with evict_last, plus flushed lines. Since r6 showed only a tiny gain, that suggests it isn't using evict_last for its stores -- I want to check the r6-s-ldef-nc-disp kernel directly to confirm, along with r3-os-l2pf for comparison. There's also the possibility that L2's address hashing across the two 63MB partitions is routing writes in a way that affects what's retained, though that shouldn't fundamentally change the picture. I'll pull up the r6-s-ldef-nc-disp kernel source to check.

reasoning_details.text:
The retention hypothesis isn't holding up either. Computing marginal bandwidth across different rented B200 memory sizes gives roughly 7 TB/s consistently at the larger sizes, but it drops off at smaller sizes, suggesting something else is going on.

I'm wondering if 7 TB/s is the actual physical ceiling given mixed read/write overhead against the 8 TB/s unlocked peak, or if there's room to improve by reducing DRAM write traffic or dirty cache line evictions during the measurement window. Testing whether avoiding eviction of dirty flush lines changes anything at the larger size didn't show a difference, so I'm not sure the L2 is behaving the way I expect.

Comparing portal (locked clocks) vs rented (unlocked) results shows the fixed-cost component growing disproportionately at lower SM clock speeds for small/medium sizes — likely because launch and CTA scheduling overhead scales with SM clock. I'm working out the CTA math for the medium case: with 49152 rows and tile size 3072, that gives 6144 CTAs total, and with 148 SMs each holding 8 resident CTAs that's 1184 resident CTAs per wave, meaning roughly 5.2 waves — so there's a partial tail wave that could explain some of the extra fixed latency.

For the large case, the same math gives about 41.5 waves, and the tail there is likely just the last CTA's lifetime (roughly 1.5-2 µs, latency-bound rather than size-bound), so shrinking CTA size wouldn't help since DRAM latency dominates regardless. That leaves the remaining medium-case overhead as essentially unavoidable launch/latency cost, and the large case is already near its bandwidth ceiling, so squeezing out another 5% at either size looks difficult — maybe L2 prefetching could help increase effective bandwidth, though I'd need to think through how.

Each CTA reads contiguous 8 KB chunks across Q then K, with writes going to a dense Qo region, so the read/write streams themselves stay locality-friendly. The real issue might be write-back scattering: with evict_last, L2 eviction order is replacement-policy-driven and fairly random across sets, which could scatter write-backs across DRAM rows and hurt write-side row-buffer efficiency.

With only a handful of experiment attempts left, I'm weighing a few cheap options — combining evict_last stores with evict_first loads plus a prefetch issued one wave ahead, or restructuring to fuse Q/K access per CTA so each CTA reads its Q tile together with the corresponding K tile.

I should also reconsider the real goal: the timing window matters because outputs still resident in L2 get written back after the kernel ends, so I need to think about what's actually sitting in cache at the finish line. If the last chunk of output could be guaranteed to stay in L2 until that moment, that might matter more than optimizing mid-kernel traffic — though retention limits mean only so much survives anyway.

Running the numbers for the 100.7 MB case at 16.4 µs: if outputs were fully retained, a pure 50 MB read would only need about 10 µs, so clearly the writes are actually happening during the window. That raises the question of whether dirty zero-initialized allocations are being evicted and adding extra write traffic, but a 50R+100W combination implies an impossible 11 TB/s, so the zero pages must not be dirty or are elided somehow — more likely the 50R+50W scenario holds, implying outputs are substantially written out within the timed window itself.

I'm testing this hypothesis by checking whether input allocations recycle dirty flush buffer lines versus evicting them separately, and the EF-load test only shows a weak effect (roughly 1-6% improvement), suggesting that recycling isn't really happening effectively.

Reducing the L2 footprint for inputs to zero isn't feasible since all loads pass through L2, so I'm shifting focus to write-back behavior — if L2 proactively flushes dirty lines, that would explain why retention gains are modest. This points to the real bottleneck being per-SM latency or fixed overhead at locked clock speeds rather than cache policy, since M still runs 13% slower than the rented baseline even with L matching.

So I'm checking whether SM throughput itself is the limiter: computing instructions per warp, bytes per clock needed versus scheduler issue capacity, and I find the SM can issue far more bandwidth than the 36 B/clk requirement, ruling out issue-bound stalls. That pushes me toward CTA launch/dispatch rate as the likely culprit at locked clocks.

Checking CTA launch rate across M and L sizes, I get similar per-SM intervals (~0.3-0.6 µs), and persistent kernels with fewer, bigger CTAs performed worse without prefetch, so this angle seems neutral rather than decisive. Given the weak signal, I'm weighing a small but measured win from EF loads across sizes, though it's marginal for M/L; I consider trying L2 prefetching a wave ahead, but that overlaps with an approach already ruled out as a repeat. That leads me to a new angle: examining tile launch order and what's resident in L2 near the end of a one-shot grid dispatch.

Thinking about whether early vs late output writes should get different cache hints -- marking early outputs evict-first for prompt, address-ordered writeback to DRAM (better streaming locality) while reserving evict-last for later outputs, since LRU behavior among evict-last lines probably just keeps the most recent ones anyway and doesn't obviously help.

I want to test tagging only the last ~96 MB of outputs (by tile index) as evict-last, with earlier outputs left at default policy and loads still marked evict-first, then compare performance against the all-evict-last baseline.

Another angle is L2 prefetch, but that's already covered by an existing A100-only variant, so it's not a distinct idea. I also consider interleaving Q and K launches so outputs and inputs alternate temporally, but that shouldn't meaningfully change DRAM traffic — it's essentially neutral. Let me try one more concrete idea: have each CTA issue a prefetch instruction for a tile one full wave ahead, using a single thread to prefetch into L2 before the loads happen.
